findings.source_passage: So we go, who file old jaws and shinbones. Let's try another. Aye, now, this works better (_sneezes_). Halloa, this bone dust is (_sneezes_)—why it's (_sneezes_)—yes it's (_sneezes_)—bless my soul, it won't let me speak!
findings.why_it_matters: The carpenter's sneezing monologue is one of the most stylistically distinctive passages in the chapter — the stage-direction sneezes embedded in the prose, the comic rhythm, and 'who file old jaws and shinbones' all establish register. The draft reduces this to a single quoted line and skips the rest entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'So we go, who file old jaws and shinbones' and at least one sneezing interjection to preserve the comic voice-establishing texture of the carpenter's opening.

findings.source_passage: I could turn him out as neat a leg now as ever (_sneezes_) scraped to a lady in a parlor. Those buckskin legs and calves of legs I've seen in shop windows wouldn't compare at all.
findings.why_it_matters: This passage carries the carpenter's eccentric craftsman pride and grotesque humor — a key voice-establishing digression that distinguishes him as a character rather than a mere foil. The draft drops it entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Include the 'scraped to a lady in a parlor' line and the shop-window comparison to restore the carpenter's comic register.

findings.source_passage: I like a good grip; I like to feel something in this slippery world that can hold, man.
findings.source_locator: Ahab's speech after feeling the vice grip
findings.why_it_matters: This is an interpretively weighty Ahab line — 'something in this slippery world that can hold' resonates thematically with Ahab's grip on purpose and obsession. It is absent from the draft entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore Ahab's line 'I like to feel something in this slippery world that can hold, man' when he grips the vice.

findings.source_passage: Hist, then. How dost thou know that some entire, living, thinking thing may not be invisibly and uninterpenetratingly standing precisely where thou now standest; aye, and standing there in thy spite? In thy most solitary hours, then, dost thou not fear eavesdroppers?
findings.source_locator: Ahab's philosophical speech to the carpenter
findings.why_it_matters: The word 'uninterpenetratingly' and the phrase 'standing there in thy spite' and 'dost thou not fear eavesdroppers' are all compressed away. These are critically engaged passages — the uncanny presence, the philosophical challenge — and the draft flattens the distinctive diction.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'uninterpenetratingly,' 'standing there in thy spite,' and 'dost thou not fear eavesdroppers' verbatim; these are the interpretive cruxes of the passage.

findings.source_passage: Look, pudding-heads should never grant premises.—How long before the leg is done?
findings.source_locator: Ahab's closing exchange before his soliloquy
findings.why_it_matters: The draft has 'Look ye, pudding-heads should never grant premises' correctly but omits 'Look ye' at the start — minor but the rhetorical flavor is slightly softened.
findings.suggested_fix: Minor — retain 'Look ye' at the head of the line.

summary: The draft faithfully preserves Ahab's major speeches and the Carpenter's closing monologue verbatim, but erases the carpenter's voice-establishing opening monologue (sneezing, craftsman pride), drops the interpretively significant 'slippery world' grip line, and compresses away the distinctive diction of Ahab's uncanny-presence speech — three medium-severity failures that together trigger regeneration.
